newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Close-up: Wik worries.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-OPINION-Jim Middleton's Canberra Close-up: Wik worries.

text.p: By Jim Middleton (ABC TV Political Correspondent)
"... the biggest challenge we have at the moment is to get the Wik issue right," John Howard said.
He can say that again. As it was for Paul Keating, so it is for his successor.
The consequences of the Mabo decision overwhelmed the decision making-processes of the previous Labor government.

Mr Keating hoped his resolution of native title would be the end of the matter, although his own statements about the impact of Aboriginal rights on pastoral leases make it clear there were significant doubts that it would actually do the trick.
And so it was that shortly before Christmas the High Court brought down its judgement in the Wik case.
John Howard's worst fears were realised.

His hope that the full bench would find that pastoral leases extinguished native title evaporated and the prime minister is left with a problem every bit as intractable and divisive as was Mabo to the man he'd seen off at the polls.
In retrospect, it seems quixotic ever to have imagined that through Wik the High Court could make life easy for the current government.

A cursory reading of the majority Toohey judgement makes it clear that right from the start of European settlement in Australia the British colonial authorities were determined to ensure that the grant of pastoral leases would not impinge on customary Aboriginal use of the land.
The tension produced by the squatters' demands for land tenure and the authorities' determination to maintain indigenous land rights remains to this day.
This is what English Secretary of State Earl Grey had to say in a despatch to New South Wales Governor Sir Charles Fitzroy in 1848:

"...these leases are not intended to deprive the natives of their former right to hunt over these districts, or to wander over them in search of subsistence, in the manner to which they have heretofore accustomed..."
Not much room for interpretation there.

Mining companies seem to acknowledge the implications of such directions and of the Wik decision -- that, as in other parts of the world, indigenous land rights are a matter for negotiation not for abolition.
Howard's problem is that it's a reality the other most affected group (apart from the Aboriginal community) -- the farmers and graziers -- will not accept.
The National Farmers' Federation -- with president Donald McGauchie leading the charge -- has taken the hardest of lines.

Extinguishment -- is his clarion call -- nothing less will do. Yesterday's agreement to codification of statutory Aboriginal and pastoralists' rights -- but only after abolition of common law native title rights -- is unconvincing subterfuge.

McGauchie seems impervious to the fact that extinguishment would ensure a further High Court challenge because it would contravene the Racial Discrimination Act and may offend the Constitution to boot.
That hardly seems to provide the certainty for pastoralists that the federation also demands.
Nor does it give any assistance to a government doing its best to find a way of meeting conflicting and contradictory demands without inviting further High Court action.
An "agreed" solution, as the prime minister puts it.
Then there's the National Party, not forgetting Rob Borbidge, Richard Court and Shane Stone. All have taken up the federation call to arms with gusto.
Parliamentary National Party mutterings turned to rebellion this week.
Queensland's Bill O'Chee is threatening to cross the floor in the Senate and resign from the coalition -- a move which would divest the government of its Senate majority.

Nationals' Senate Leader Ron Boswell declares flatly that codification won't work and that there's no support on the coalition backbench -- Liberals included -- for anything other than extinguishment.
Thus far Howard has been standing firm.
He won't, he insists, let the farmers down.
Equally, declares the prime minister, he has a responsibility to govern "fairly" for the Aboriginal community.
And he appears to be as good as his word.
Last night, Wik dominated Howard's pre-premiers conference dinner with the state leaders.
This morning Rob Borbidge and Richard Court signalled their displeasure with the direction Howard is heading on Wik -- a sure sign the prime minister is planning something less than extinguishment.
The question is just how limited his codified rights would be and how broad a right to negotiate over future development Aborigines would enjoy.
But, as with guns, it seems Howard won't be moved -- not by the premiers, not by his own backbench and certainly not by the NFF.
The federation's claims to be seeking a workable solution look even less credible today after the airing of its inflammatory TV commercials on the subject.
Images of black and white boys fighting on a Twister board with a black hand claiming a "white" circle hardly helps the struggle towards an "agreed" solution.
The prime minister will not be pleased.
-- Reuters Canberra Bureau 61-6 273-2730
